extracted.intended_audience: graduate students in mathematics (Master's and Ph.D.) at the University of Lethbridge
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and writing a Master’s or Ph.D. thesis in mathematics, covering required originality, attribution, citation style, copyright, formatting, and use of LaTeX. Targets both research and expository theses and explains university policy implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis must make a contribution and report prior knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Your thesis must make a contribution to some field of mathematics, and also report what was previously known about the topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General requirement for both Master's and Ph.D. degrees: the thesis must contain original student research work (university policy references given). The thesis should both advance the field and give an account of earlier results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ph.D. expectation: significant original research
rubrics_metrics.description: A Ph.D. thesis is expected to have a significant amount of original mathematical research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This will normally include at least one substantial theorem that was not previously known. The department expects substantial original results as part of a doctoral thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master's thesis: research-based or expository
rubrics_metrics.description: A master's thesis may either be research-based or expository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A research-based thesis has new theorems like a Ph.D. thesis. An expository thesis mainly explains known results but to meet the university requirement that 'the Thesis must consist of original student research work', an expository thesis must provide new insights (e.g., a different approach, additional examples/applications, omitted proofs, or connections between fields).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plagiarism: attribute every idea from others
rubrics_metrics.description: Every idea that came from someone else must be specifically attributed to the correct source; representing others' words, ideas, images or data as your own is plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you state a theorem/lemma/definition/etc. in your thesis without giving a reference, you are claiming it as new. Plagiarism is a very serious offence with severe penalties including rejection of the thesis. You will be penalized even if the violation was unintentional. Follow university Graduate Studies Calendar regulations and library guidance on when to cite.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to cite / When not to cite
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite whenever you present words, ideas, images, or data of someone else; no citation is needed if the wording and idea are your own or if the fact is common knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paraphrases require citation because the idea is not yours. Most citation styles require both an in-text citation and a bibliography entry. If an idea or fact is widespread disciplinary common knowledge you may omit a citation, but when in doubt, cite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation and paraphrase rules
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot use another person's words exactly without quotation marks (or equivalent formatting) and attribution; paraphrases must be your own wording, not small edits of the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simply changing a few words or rearranging words is still plagiarism. Paraphrasing demands thorough understanding and substantially different sentence/paragraph structure. Technical terms may be reused without quotes, but distinctive phrases should not be copied. Use quotation marks or block quotes for literal text and always cite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics-specific quotation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks are rare in mathematical writing for technical material such as theorem statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to copy a theorem statement verbatim (without quotation marks) provided you give the appropriate reference. Use judgment whether to copy a theorem word-for-word or adapt it to match your notation and exposition. Explanatory prose should not be copied verbatim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect copyright and obtain permissions when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright restricts how much text/figures can be copied from a source even with citation; permission is required when exceeding legal/owner allowances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a guideline the APA (cited) suggests: a maximum of three figures/tables from a journal/book chapter, single text extracts under 400 words, or a series of extracts totalling under 800 words. If you need more, obtain permission from the copyright owner; permission can be refused or delayed. Prefer writing original exposition rather than copying large sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-plagiarism / duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: You must not submit all or a substantial portion of prior academic work without knowledge and approval of recipients; duplication is disallowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot reuse undergraduate or other previously-credited work as original content in your graduate thesis (e.g., Ph.D. cannot reproduce Master's thesis). If related prior work should be included as background, clearly mark it as such. It is acceptable to include results from your published papers if the work was done as part of your current graduate studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement to publish and include published results
rubrics_metrics.description: A thesis is stronger if it includes theorems already published (or accepted) in reputable journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your thesis contains new theorems, you are encouraged to publish them in a journal. Published work done as part of the current graduate studies may be included in the thesis as original content.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to refer to bibliography items (citation format guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, the usual style is to use item numbers in square brackets, followed by specific location information such as theorem number and page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'A. Zmith [99, Proposition 2.1, p. 5]...' or 'Theorem 2 (Zmith [99, Proposition 2.1, p. 5]).' Page numbers can be omitted for short papers but references must be specific enough for the reader to locate the cited material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and preparation: use LaTeX and department template
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare your thesis in LaTeX and use the department-supplied LaTeX template to satisfy university formatting requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LaTeX is the world-wide standard for mathematics papers and is installed on department computers. Learn to use the \cite macro to make references to your bibliography. The department template and university policies cited (sections on formatting) should be followed for detailed formatting requirements.
